lines.text: TRIBE TRIPHOREAE DRESSLER
18. Psilochilus Barb. Rodr.
Terrestrial or epiphytic, plants with creeping rhi-
zomes. Roots adventitious, fleshy. Leaves membrana-
ceous with lax petioles. Inflorescences terminal, a
short spicate raceme. Flowers few. Sepals free,
keeled along the mid-vein. Petals free, not keeled
along mid-vein. Lip free, 3-lobed; disc with 3 longi-
tudinal calli. Column elongate, clavate; anther ter-
minal, 2-celled, mobile; pollinia 4.
This is a monotypic genus of tropical America.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek psilo (smooth) and
chilus (lipped) in reference to the appearance of the
lip.
Psilochilus macrophyllus (Lindl.) Ames, Orch.
Fasc. 7: 45 (1922). Type: locality unknown, Linden
(holo. K-LINDL.!).
Pogonia macrophylla Lindl. in Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist.
P. physurifolia Rchb. f. in Nederl. Kruidk. Arch. 4:
Plant terrestrial or epiphytic, with fleshy roots. Stem
branched, ascending. Leaves rigid, membranaceous,
oval-elliptic, up to 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence terminal, racemose, 1- to 2-flowered; bracts
leafy, up to 2 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Flowers
ringent with greenish sepals, greenish- white petals
and white lip. Sepals stiff and fleshy; dorsal sepal up
to 1.9 cm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals up to 1.8
cm long and 3 mm wide. Petals thinner than the
sepals, up to 1.8 cm long and 3 mm wide. Lip
3-lobed, up to 1.6 cm long and 8 mm wide; lateral
lobes acute; mid-lobe with serrate margins. Column
with 2 conspicuous broad apical teeth on the side of
the rostellum. (Fig. 18).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Central
America to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On leaf litter over sandy soil on the
forest floor and on mossy tree branches about 3 m
above the ground.
FLOWERING SEASON. December.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek macrophyllus
(large-leaved).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).
18 Psilochilus
SUBTRIBE VANILLINAE LINDL.
19. Epistephium Kunth
Terrestrial herbs. Stems tall, simple or branched. Lea-
ves chartaceous to coriaceous, usually sessile or
cordate-clasping, strongly veined. Inflorescences ter-
minal or, rarely, axillary, racemose, many-flowered.
Flowers large; bracts short; apex of ovary with an
urceolate cup. Sepals subequal, free. Petals rather
similar to sepals but sometimes larger. Lip adnate to
the column, obovate, simple or slightly 3-lobed, en-
clasping the base of the column. Column long, dilated
above, broadly 3-lobed at apex. Capsule oblong-
cylindric.
A genus of about 20 species known from Belize,
Trinidad and northern South America. One is known
from Belize.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Greek epi (upon, above)
and stefos (a crown, wreath) in reference to the
crown-like growth that remains at the apex of the
ovary.
Epistephium ellipticum R.O. Williams & Summerh.
in Kew Bull.: 145 (1928). Type: Trinidad, Freeman,
Williams & Cheesman (holo. TRIN; iso. K!).
Epistephium tenuifolium Mansf. ex Hoehne, Fl. Bra-
E minutum Barb.-Rodr. ex Hoehne, Fl. Brasilica
Plant terrestrial, erect, up to 30 cm tall, with fleshy
roots and simple stems of up to 3 mm in diameter.
Leaves thinly coriaceous, glabrous, veins rather
prominent on both sides, short-petiolate, elliptic or
oblong-elliptic, abruptly acute or acuminate, basally
narrowed, up to 6.5 cm long and 3 cm wide. Inflores-
cence terminal or axillary, racemose, shorter than the
leaves, up to 12-flowered. Flowers green; ovary ar-
cuate, slightly trigonous, up to 4 cm long; bracts
triangular, acuminate, persisting in fruit. Sepals spa-
thulate, acute, up to 2 cm long and 3 mm wide. Petals
spathulate, up to 2 cm long and 4 mm wide, white.
Lip with lower clasping and adnate to the column,
upper ⅓ dilated, rotundate in outline, entire, ex-
panded portion up to 8 mm long, ciliate, upper half
flesly-pilose. Column up to 17 mm long and 1.5 mm
in diameter. Capsule linear-cylindric, up to 3.5 cm
long and 2 mm in diameter. (Fig. 19).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Belize,
Venezuela, Brazil and Trinidad.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (Mountain Pine
